![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216490/assets/09a38bb4306728f97b7fecbf9ab1bda7aa957607352c1ab27af09489c271c3ed.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}({y}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(2,3),$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,1)$ and $(2,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(0+t(2-0)),\,(1+t(3-1))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,1+2t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-2x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+2t)^{2}-2(2t) \\  & =1+4t+4{t}^{2}-4t \\  & =4{t}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{[\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2(\frac{4}{3}+1)-2(0) \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
